In Java, the short answer is no: List<String> is not a subclass of List<Object>. This is a common point of friction for developers transitioning from languages with different variance models. The reason lies in Java's invariant generic type system. If List<String> were a subtype of List<Object>, you could perform a heap-polluting operation: you could pass a List<String> to a method expecting a List<Object>, and that method could then insert an Integer into the list. When the original code attempts to retrieve a String from its list, the JVM would throw a ClassCastException at runtime. To prevent this, Java enforces invariance at compile-time: the generic type parameter must match exactly.

Generics covariance is handled via wildcards. When you use List<? extends Object>, you are declaring a covariant relationship. This tells the compiler that the collection holds some unknown type that is a subtype of Object. However, this comes with a trade-off: the 'Producer Extends, Consumer Super' (PECS) principle. Because the compiler cannot verify the exact type being inserted, it prevents you from adding elements to a covariant list, effectively making it read-only for the generic type.

rows: Cannot guarantee type safety for insertion

items: Type Erasure: At runtime, both List<String> and List<Object> are reduced to raw List types, meaning the JVM has no concept of the generic type parameter. The compiler performs all checks during the compilation phase to ensure type safety.

Heap Pollution: This occurs when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type. Invariance is the primary guardrail against this, ensuring that the reference type and the object type remain consistent.

PECS Principle: If you need to read from a collection, use ? extends T (Producer). If you need to write to a collection, use ? super T (Consumer). This allows for flexible API design without breaking the type system.

parsed_answer.content: Watch out for the 'Raw Type' trap. If you assign a List<String> to a raw List, you bypass all generic type checking. This is a legacy feature for backward compatibility that effectively disables the compiler's ability to protect you from ClassCastExceptions. Always treat raw types as a code smell in production codebases.

title: Is List<String> a subclass of List<Object>? (Generics covariance)
